q: A DC node receives 2.40 A and sends 1.35 A through one branch. Determine its other outgoing current and its value if input rises by 0.15 A.
model: Steady lumped node, charge accumulation zero, positive currents directed into the junction.
calc: By KCL, +2.40−1.35−I₂=0 A, hence I₂=1.05 A outward.
check: Over 2 s, 4.80 C enters and 2.70+2.10=4.80 C leaves; independent integrated balance is zero.
change: With input 2.55 A and first output fixed, the missing exit becomes 1.20 A.
fallacy: Do not sum all branches as positive without a sign convention; that produces a false 4.80 A residual.
scope: Instrument skew, hidden branches and transient storage may mimic a nonzero observed residual.

q: Are simultaneous inputs 0.85 A and 0.65 A compatible with outgoing 1.10 A and 0.40 A at one steady node?
model: Four labeled arrows terminate at a single ideal node; the readings are contemporaneous.
calc: Signed sum=(0.85+0.65)−(1.10+0.40)=0.00 A. Input and output both equal 1.50 A.
check: In 10 s, 15.0 C enters and 15.0 C leaves, independently meeting charge conservation.
change: An extra 0.20 A exit with inputs fixed yields −0.20 A residual, so the four readings cannot all remain steady.
fallacy: Zero KCL residual does not establish safe wire temperature or source-current capacity.
scope: Transient accumulation and sensor bias need checking before assigning any specific physical fault.

q: An ideal loop has a +15 V source rise and successive drops of 4 V, 6 V and 5 V. Why is its signed sum zero?
model: Travel from source negative to positive, then traverse each passive drop; no time-varying linked flux.
calc: KVL gives +15−4−6−5=0 V; drops total 15 V.
check: For each coulomb, +15 J source work equals 4+6+5=15 J dissipated or stored by elements.
change: Changing only the measured 6 V drop to 7 V produces a −1 V arithmetic discrepancy requiring remeasurement.
fallacy: Adding all magnitudes gives 30 V, which is not a signed loop sum.
scope: Induced electromotive force must be included if the linked magnetic flux changes.

q: Calculate current and separate drops in an 18 V series circuit with 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors; repeat when 4 Ω becomes 7 Ω.
model: Ideal DC supply, two steady ohmic series loads, negligible wire and source resistance.
check: Power delivered 18×3=54 W equals I²(2+4)=54 W.
change: R_total=2+7=9 Ω, I=2 A; the new drops 4 V and 14 V sum to 18 V.
fallacy: Equal series current does not mean equal series resistor voltage.
scope: Resistor self-heating and source droop are excluded; a physical circuit needs power ratings.

q: An ideal capacitor stores 150 µC on one plate at 10 V. What is its capacitance, and what plate charge follows at 6 V?
model: Constant-geometry linear dielectric; Q is magnitude on ONE plate, not sum of signed charges.
check: Charge ratio 90/150=0.60 equals voltage ratio 6/10.
change: Holding the 15 µF capacitance fixed while decreasing voltage to 6 V reduces charge magnitude to 90 µC.
fallacy: Zero total charge across both opposite plates does not imply zero stored energy or capacitance.
scope: Strongly voltage-dependent dielectrics or leakage can invalidate the fixed-capacitance approximation.

q: Compute stored field energy of a 33 µF ideal capacitor at 9 V, then at 12 V without changing capacitance.
model: Isolated linear capacitor with fixed C; no claim that 12 V meets a real component voltage rating.
calc: Integrating V=q/C gives U=½CV²; U₉=½×33×10⁻⁶×81=1.3365 mJ.
change: Increasing voltage 9→12 V adds 1.0395 mJ, exceeding a linear 4/3 scaling.
fallacy: CV has dimensions coulombs, not joules, so it is not the capacitor-energy equation.
scope: Dielectric breakdown, ESR heating and leakage are absent from this stored-energy model.

q: For a 2.0 kΩ–100 µF ideal discharge initially at 10 V, find τ and voltage at t=τ; repeat at the same time after doubling R.
model: Unpowered RC discharge with no leakage or instrument loading, t=0 at disconnection.
calc: C dV/dt=−V/R integrates to V₀exp(−t/RC); τ=2000×100 µF=0.200 s; V(τ)=3.6788 V.
check: The exponential factor exp(−1)=0.367879, and Ω·F has dimensions seconds.
change: Doubling R gives τ=0.400 s, so at absolute t=0.200 s voltage is 10exp(−0.5)=6.0653 V.
fallacy: A time constant does NOT mean full discharge; approximately 36.8% voltage remains.
scope: Real capacitors have ESR and leakage; a voltmeter can change the observed τ.

q: How strongly do +2 nC and −3 nC point charges attract at 0.30 m in vacuum, and what changes at 0.60 m?
model: Static isolated point charges, vacuum k≈8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², center-to-center separation.
check: At 0.60 m the force is one quarter, 1.4983×10⁻⁷ N; opposite signs imply attraction.
change: Doubling distance reduces magnitude by factor four while preserving the attracting direction.
fallacy: An inverse-distance model incorrectly predicts half, not a quarter, of the initial force.
scope: Finite charged conductors with induction cannot be treated as isolated point charges near their surfaces.

q: Two +4 nC and +5 nC charges are 0.20 m apart. Calculate the repulsive force on each and compare at 0.40 m.
model: Stationary vacuum point charges, only mutual electrostatic interaction.
check: Newton third-law force vectors are opposite but each has magnitude 4.495 µN.
change: At 0.40 m, each force magnitude is 1.12375 µN, still repulsive.
fallacy: Different source charges do not imply different magnitudes of their mutual forces.
scope: Nearby third charges or geometry of real conductors would change the two-body result.

q: What radial electric field exists 0.50 m from a lone +5 nC source in vacuum, and what is its field at 1.00 m?
model: Small static source charge and infinitesimal nonperturbing positive test charge define field.
calc: E=kQ/r²=8.99×10⁹×5×10⁻⁹/(0.50²)=179.8 N/C radially outward.
check: At 1.00 m, field is 44.95 N/C, exactly one quarter of 179.8.
change: Double the detector radius, and E falls to 44.95 N/C with unchanged outward direction.
fallacy: Field is not multiplied by a chosen test charge; test charge affects force F=qE, not prescribed E.
scope: The r→0 singularity is unphysical for a finite source; electrode geometry also matters.

q: Given E_x=−200 N/C, what signed x-force acts on a −3 µC charge and on a +3 µC charge?
model: Uniform external electric field with +x to the right; test charges do not perturb it.
calc: F_x=qE_x=(−3×10⁻⁶)(−200)=+6.0×10⁻⁴ N for the negative charge.
check: C×N/C=N; a negative charge experiences force opposite to the negative field direction.
change: Changing only the test charge to +3 µC changes F_x to −6.0×10⁻⁴ N.
fallacy: A negative field component does not imply a negative force for a negative charge.
scope: Force on a test charge is not necessarily acceleration direction if non-electric forces act.

q: An ideal +0.020 C charge experiences +0.60 N along x. Infer E_x and predict the force if charge sign reverses.
model: Formal field-definition exercise with fixed external E; 20 mC is not claimed to be a nonperturbing real probe.
check: Substitution 30 N/C×0.020 C reproduces +0.60 N and correct dimensions.
change: Reversing only charge sign reverses force, not the external field.
fallacy: Electric field is force per unit charge, not a force that remains identical for different q.
scope: In a realistic geometry such a large probe charge could alter the source-field distribution.

q: A +3 mC probe loses 0.015 J potential energy from A to B. Compute V_B−V_A and the electric field's work.
model: Electrostatic conservative field, fixed endpoints, signed +q, ΔU=U_B−U_A.
check: Reconstruct qΔV=0.003×(−5)=−0.015 J; ΔU+W_field=0.
change: Replacing q with −3 mC at unchanged ΔV reverses ΔU to +0.015 J and field work to −0.015 J.
fallacy: Negative potential-energy change does not always mean negative voltage when probe charge is negative.
scope: Electrostatic potential difference may not capture nonconservative induction in varying fields.

q: A −2.0 mC charge gains 0.010 J potential energy from A to B. Is point B higher or lower in electric potential?
model: Charge algebraic sign is negative, electrostatic endpoints fixed and probe small.
check: qΔV=(−0.0020)(−5)=+0.010 J confirms the sign and units.
change: Using +2 mC at identical endpoints yields ΔU=−0.010 J with the same −5 V point-to-point difference.
fallacy: Positive ΔU does not necessarily mean positive ΔV: divide by the signed q.
scope: Probes are idealized and do not alter the electrode/source geometry.

q: A +4 µC test charge crosses a +12 V potential rise. Find ΔU and compare with a −4 µC test charge.
model: Conservative electrostatic field, V_B−V_A=+12 V, fixed A and B.
calc: ΔU=qΔV=4×10⁻⁶×12=+48 µJ for the positive charge; W_field=−48 µJ.
check: Dimension C×(J/C)=J; field work plus potential-energy change sums to zero.
change: For −4 µC, ΔU=−48 µJ and field work=+48 µJ while endpoint voltage remains +12 V.
fallacy: Potential in volts is energy per coulomb and must not be reported as total joules.
scope: No claim about particle acceleration or time-varying electromagnetic induction.

q: A junction receives 0.75 A and sends 0.25 A and 0.30 A to two loads; determine current and 60-second transported charge in a third exit.
model: Steady four-branch node with all outgoing directions specified.
check: 45 C enters in 60 s and outputs 15 C+18 C+12 C=45 C.
change: Increasing second branch to 0.40 A leaves only 0.10 A for third branch.
fallacy: The supplied 0.75 A is not the current in every outgoing parallel branch.
scope: Demanded branch currents may be infeasible without valid underlying source and component models.

q: A steady node receives 3.60 A and sends 1.80 A and 0.90 A into two branches. Determine the required third output.
model: Three stated currents simultaneous with dQ_node/dt=0 assumed.
calc: I₃=3.60−1.80−0.90=0.90 A outgoing; total outflow 3.60 A.
check: If third output were absent and other values stayed fixed, dQ_node/dt=+0.90 C/s, contradicting a sustained steady state.
change: Removing the branch requires other currents or node voltage to change; the assumed values cannot remain steady indefinitely.
fallacy: Nonzero hypothetical KCL residual does not overturn charge conservation, it overturns the steady imposed-current model.
scope: Real transient node capacitance can temporarily accumulate charge.

q: Two current sources feed a node at 0.50 A and 0.70 A; one output is 0.65 A. What is its second output and why not its node voltage?
model: Ideal simultaneous branch-current specification, with no I–V relations or ground-reference details.
calc: I₂=0.50+0.70−0.65=0.55 A; total 1.20 A enters and leaves.
check: In 20 s, 24 C enter, 13 C leave via the first output, and 11 C via the second.
change: Decreasing only the 0.70 A input to 0.60 A reduces required second outflow to 0.45 A.
fallacy: Charge balance alone cannot determine voltage without resistances, source models and node reference.
scope: Independent ideal current sources may be incompatible with actual topology; verify complete circuit constraints.

q: A 9 V battery drives 2 Ω and 4 Ω series loads. Derive I, each resistor drop and total power.
model: Ideal source with constant ohmic loads and one conventional-current loop.
calc: R_total=6 Ω; I=9/6=1.5 A; drops are 3 V and 6 V with +9−3−6=0.
check: Source power 9×1.5=13.5 W equals I²×2 + I²×4=4.5+9.0 W.
change: Replacing 4 Ω by 8 Ω gives I=0.9 A with drops 1.8 V and 7.2 V.
fallacy: Same current in series does not imply identical voltage drops for unequal resistors.
scope: Self-heating and battery internal resistance are ignored, not proven absent.

q: A loop records +24 V source and 8 V, 7 V and 9 V drops. Is it consistent, and what if the first drop reads 9 V?
model: All measurements simultaneous under a declared traversal and sign convention.
calc: Loop residual δV=+24−8−7−9=0 V; listed values satisfy ideal KVL.
check: For each coulomb, 24 J gained balances 24 J of electrical potential drops.
change: If the first drop changes to 9 V with other readings fixed, residual is −1 V and the model or measurements need checking.
fallacy: A −1 V residual is not proof that 1 J per coulomb literally disappeared.
scope: Check meter polarity, reading simultaneity and induced emf before assigning hardware failure.

q: For a constant 9 V ideal source and 3.0 kΩ resistor, calculate DC current and power, then double R.
model: Steady temperature-independent ohmic device with ideal fixed voltage.
check: P=I²R=(0.003)²×3000=0.027 W matches V²/R.
change: At 6.0 kΩ, I=1.5 mA and P=13.5 mW, exactly half under fixed V.
fallacy: Do not double current when doubling resistance with fixed voltage.
scope: A diode or self-heating resistor may not maintain constant R.

q: A synthetic device measures 5 V at 20 mA. Find its point resistance and power; what extra assumption predicts current at 10 V?
model: Single measured operating point; constant resistance at other voltages is NOT established.
calc: R_point=5/0.020=250 Ω and P=VI=0.10 W.
check: IR=0.020×250=5.0 V and I²R=(0.02)²×250=0.10 W independently confirm.
change: Only IF R stays 250 Ω, at 10 V current is 40 mA and power 0.40 W.
fallacy: A single V/I observation does not prove a diode or nonlinear sensor is ohmic.
scope: Thermal and nonlinear effects require a measured I–V curve before extrapolation.

q: A resistor reports simultaneous 12.0 V and 0.300 A. Determine point resistance and power, then conditionally predict 6 V behavior.
model: Synthetic reading; constant R over a changed voltage requires an explicit extra assumption.
check: I²R=0.300²×40=3.60 W and unit analysis gives V/A=Ω.
change: If R stays 40 Ω, at 6 V current is 0.150 A and power only 0.900 W.
fallacy: Voltage divided by current is resistance in ohms, not power in watts.
scope: A 3.6 W dissipation can strongly heat an actual resistor and change R.

q: Place ideal 4 µF and 6 µF capacitors in parallel across 5 V. Find charge on each positive plate, total C and stored energy.
model: Both parallel devices share 5 V and have ideal linear dielectrics; use charge magnitude on ONE electrode per capacitor.
calc: C_eq=4+6=10 µF, Q₁=20 µC, Q₂=30 µC, Q_total=50 µC; U=½×10 µF×25=125 µJ.
check: Independent energies ½×4 µF×25=50 µJ and ½×6 µF×25=75 µJ sum to 125 µJ.
change: In series at 5 V, C_eq=2.4 µF, both equal 12 µC charge magnitude, total energy 30 µJ.
fallacy: Series capacitors share equal charge, parallel capacitors share equal voltage; swapping these rules gives wrong results.
scope: Voltage ratings, discharge losses, polarity and leakage require separate checks.
